# Policy Compiler Principles {.unnumbered}

Parts I through IV built an architecture around a fixed model. Part V changes the model. In the Stochastic Computer this is the compiler, which turns the trajectories the runtime has logged into a policy that proposes better actions. Changing the model moves none of the three H·S·A exposures. A retrained policy runs the same horizon, carries the same state, and holds the same zero ambient authority, so every envelope, log, and gate of Parts II through IV stays in force. What training can change is how often the model's proposals pass those gates. Retraining is therefore the last rung of repair, reached only after missing context, unclear interfaces, and runtime faults have been ruled out, and the gates themselves become the source of the training signal.

::: {#pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training .callout-principle title="Verified trajectory post-training"}

**Invariant**: Changing model weights is the slowest and least reversible intervention in an agentic system, and it repairs only the failures that remain after missing context, ambiguous tool schemas, and runtime faults are ruled out. For those failures the training signal is a multi-turn trajectory that deterministic checks outside the model have accepted, including trajectories that recover from errors, because a policy that has seen only error-free paths accumulates errors as the horizon grows.

**Implication**: A harvesting pipeline triages each failure before any training run, admits a trajectory only on evidence produced outside the model, and keeps recovery traces in the corpus alongside clean ones.

:::

Once a trajectory is admitted, the loss must be aimed at the tokens the policy will actually write.

::: {#pri-vol3-action-masked-loss .callout-principle title="Observation loss masking"}

**Invariant**: In a serialized trajectory, observation tokens are written by the environment and not by the policy. Training the model to predict them spends capacity on imitating tools and teaches it to write its own observations instead of yielding the turn to the runtime.

**Implication**: The training loss covers only tokens the policy will emit when it runs, meaning its actions, the end-of-turn token that returns control to the runtime, and, when the deployment needs it, its reasoning. Prompts and observations stay in context without contributing loss, and a turn cut off before its end-of-turn token is masked or dropped.

:::

Supervised training imitates trajectories that have already passed a check. Reinforcement learning goes further and lets the policy search against the check itself.

::: {#pri-vol3-verifiable-rewards .callout-principle title="Reinforcement learning against isolated verifiers"}

**Invariant**: Reinforcement learning turns the reward check into the objective. The policy learns whatever the check rewards, including any route by which it can reach and change the check, and it learns nothing the check does not test. The gradient also vanishes unless the policy already succeeds on some attempts and fails on others.

**Implication**: An RL pipeline runs the verifier in an isolated environment that receives only the policy's output artifact, judges the trained policy on held-out tests the reward never saw, and starts from a supervised policy whose pass rate is above zero.

:::

@Sec-vol3-trajectory-curation triages failures and admits trajectories through a cascade of checks, @sec-vol3-fine-tuning trains on them with a masked loss, and @sec-vol3-rlvr optimizes against isolated verifiers. All three depend on the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}), which makes running a stated check on every trajectory affordable and leaves the soundness of that check as the limit on what training can learn. Weights change how likely a proposal is to pass, never the authority to act on it. Part VI takes the resulting agents from one trajectory to many.
